newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Wider NZ inflation target may be on agenda - Birch.
newsitem.headline: Wider NZ inflation target may be on agenda - Birch.

text.p: Finance Minister Bill Birch said on Monday that a loosening of New Zealand's 0-2 percent inflation target may be on the agenda in the National Party's coalition talks to form a government.
Asked if a loosening of the Reserve Bank of New Zealand's inflation target would be on the agenda, Birch told Reuters Financial Television: "It may well be."

"I don't want to comment on the issues that may be subject to negotiation. That's something that will emerge with time but it is something that has yet to be clarified as to what compromises, if any, are to be made," Birch said.
Asked if he could accept a case for loosening fiscal policy, Birch said he was seeking to maintain quality in expansion of spending to achieve positive outcomes.

"The Prime Minister Jim Bolger has made it very clear that we want to maintain our broad mix of policies that have performed so well to give us economic growth and a much better performance of the New Zealand economy.
"That's very much a priority for us. That's not to say there would not be some tweaking of those policies.
"We've never claimed that they're perfect, and indeed during the campaign we argued ourselves that they needed to be built on as we look ahead," Birch said.

Asked if New Zealand may still be without a government by the time parliament reconvenes on December 13, Birch said: "That is a remote possibility. I think the parties will want to try and make more progress than that and I would think they'd want to have a clear position and a government in place before the parliament convenes in early December."
He reiterated that there would be no policy changes in the interim while National continues as a caretaker government.
"I would expect that this will be a period of quiet stability...It's a time for stability in the marketplace," Birch said.
"The markets have responded in a mature way, and I think that's excellent.

"My advice to investors is that they should continue to monitor the position with confidence -- that I think at the end of the day there should be no reason other than for the investors to continue to invest in New Zealand," Birch Said.
Birch said New Zealand First had the most responsible economic and fiscal policies of the three opposition parties.
New Zealand First had positioned itself "pretty much in the centre", Birch said. "I think it's positioned itself that it could go in either direction..."

Saturday's general election produced an inconclusive result, with the conservative National Party and its allies winning 53 seats and Labour and the left-wing Alliance winning 50, leaving New Zealand First with its 17 seats holding the balance of power.
NZ First has advocated changing the Reserve Bank's target to make it aim for less than the average inflation rate of New Zealand's top 10 trading partners.
